summary: Defines a two-way mapping between SIP and XMPP for single instant messages. It allows users on one system to message users on the other.

eli5.summary: Two chat apps speak different languages. This is the translator for single short messages.

questions: how does sip to xmpp interworking work

how are xmpp stanzas mapped to sip
subtitle: How a gateway turns a single SIP instant message into an XMPP message, and back again.

tldr.problem: SIP and XMPP both carry instant messages, but they use different formats and addressing, so a user on one system cannot message a user on the other without a translator.
tldr.mechanism: A gateway maps an XMPP message stanza to a SIP MESSAGE request and the reverse, field by field, using two mapping tables. Only single, one-off messages (pager-mode) are covered.
tldr.outcome: The RFC gives developers a direct mapping for single messages, including rules for size limits, content types and language tags. Chat sessions and group chat are left to other documents.

today: RFC 7572 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Chat sessions are handled by the companion RFC 7573.

sections.title: Why a Direct Mapping
sections.content:
Two instant messaging technologies came out of the IETF. One is the Session Initiation Protocol (SIP) with its MESSAGE method extension, collectively called SIMPLE. The other is the Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol (XMPP). Both let two entities exchange an "instant message", meaning a message delivered in close to real time rather than stored and forwarded on request.

One way to connect such systems is to map each protocol to a shared abstract model, the approach of RFC 3860. This document instead maps one protocol directly to the other, because that is how existing systems solve the problem.

It covers only single messages (also called pager-mode), the lowest common denominator for instant messaging. One-to-one chat sessions are handled in RFC 7573, and the shared architecture, address mapping and error mapping come from RFC 7247.
sections.eli5: Instead of translating both chat apps into a third secret language, this document teaches each one to talk straight to the other. It only covers one-off messages, like a single text.

sections.title: From XMPP to SIP
sections.content:
A single XMPP instant message is a <message/> stanza of type normal, which is the default, so the attribute is often left out. The sender's server looks at the domain in the to address using the procedure in RFC 7247. If the domain is a SIP domain, the server hands the stanza to an XMPP-to-SIP gateway.

The gateway turns the stanza into a SIP MESSAGE request. The destination SIP server delivers it and the recipient answers with a response such as 200 OK. A proxy may fork the request, but only one 200 OK comes back to the gateway. The RFC does not say how the gateway should use that response, for example to acknowledge delivery to the XMPP user. Acknowledgements are covered in RFC 7573 for chat sessions.

The field mapping MUST follow Table 1. The XMPP type attribute has no SIP counterpart, since no SIP header matches values such as chat or headline. The gateway MUST map the sender's bare JID (localpart@domainpart) to the SIP From header, and carry the resourcepart of the full JID as the Globally Routable User Agent URI (GRUU) part of the SIP URI.
sections.eli5: When a chat message heads to a SIP user, a helper at the border rewrites the envelope in SIP style. Some labels, like the kind of message, have no matching label, so they are simply dropped.

sections.title: From SIP to XMPP
sections.content:
A single SIP instant message is a MESSAGE request. The recipient is generally named by an im: URI, but may be a sip: or sips: URI. A SIP user agent resolves an im: URI to sip: or sips:, so the RFC assumes the gateway sees one of those in the Request-URI.

The SIP server checks the domain of the Request-URI or To header. If it is an XMPP domain, the request goes to a SIP-to-XMPP gateway. The gateway builds an XMPP message stanza and returns a SIP 200 OK to the sender. The mapping MUST follow Table 2.

When the gateway knows the GRUU of the sending endpoint, it MUST map the sender to a full JID in the from attribute and use the GRUU as the resourcepart. For pager-mode messages the gateway MUST set no XMPP type, or the value normal. An XMPP server may deliver a stanza addressed to a bare JID to several connected devices, which resembles forking in SIP.
sections.eli5: Going the other way, the border helper rewrites a SIP envelope in XMPP style and tells the sender it arrived. It marks the message as an ordinary one-off note.

sections.title: Message Size Limits
sections.content:
SIP and XMPP disagree about size. RFC 3428 says a MESSAGE request outside a media session must not exceed 1300 bytes. XMPP sets no upper limit on stanza size, although deployments usually set one to resist denial-of-service attacks, and RFC 6120 says any limit a server sets must not be less than 10,000 bytes.

Because of this mismatch, an XMPP-to-SIP gateway SHOULD return a <policy-violation/> stanza error if an XMPP message would produce a SIP MESSAGE larger than 1300 bytes. A gateway might instead switch to session mode using the Message Session Relay Protocol (MSRP), but that is application-specific and the RFC gives no guidance on how.
sections.eli5: One system only accepts short notes, while the other lets you write long ones. If a note is too long to fit, the helper hands it back with a polite error.

sections.title: Content Types and Languages
sections.content:
A SIP MESSAGE may carry almost any content type. A SIP-to-XMPP gateway MUST process text/plain bodies and put them in the XMPP <body/> element as character data. It SHOULD process text/html, and if it does it MUST transform the content into XHTML that conforms to the XHTML-IM Integration Set in XEP-0071. Other types may be processed, but how is left to the implementation.

Both protocols support UTF-8 and language tagging. XMPP uses the xml:lang attribute and SIP uses the Content-Language header. Gateways MUST map these when present. The RFC's example is a Czech message tagged cs that comes out the other side with xml:lang='cs'.
sections.eli5: Plain text always gets through. Fancier formatted text is converted if the helper can manage it, and a note's language label travels along with it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC points to the security sections of the underlying specifications: RFC 2779 for instant messaging generally, RFC 3428 and RFC 3261 for SIP, RFC 6121 and RFC 6120 for XMPP, and RFC 7247 for interworking. A gateway MUST meet the minimum security requirements of the chat protocols it translates between.

Gateways add new risk. End-to-end confidentiality and integrity between clients on either side can only be provided if both sides support common formats, and defining those formats is out of scope. Two standardized methods exist, but they are not widely implemented. Off-the-Record Messaging is more widely implemented but not standardized.
sections.eli5: A translator in the middle can read the message unless both sides lock it in a way they both understand. This document does not pick that lock.
